report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **not false** — the balance of evidence supports it, though with important caveats about outdoor conditions.

## Evidence

Controlled studies consistently find that ventilating a bedroom by opening a window or door lowers carbon dioxide (CO2) accumulation, which is linked to better sleep. A Danish (Technical University of Denmark) field study found that when window ventilation kept bedroom CO2 below ~750 ppm, air quality was good enough that it no longer measurably affected sleep, and participants performed better cognitively the next day (https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day). A rigorous Dutch study using actigraphy and pillow-based movement sensors in 17 healthy young adults directly compared open vs. closed windows/doors and found that ventilation reduced CO2 and was associated with objectively measured improvements in sleep quality (https://research.aalto.fi/en/publications/windowdoor-openingmediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on-). A more recent field intervention study similarly reported that increased bedroom ventilation over four weeks improved subjective and physiological sleep quality (https://www.psypost.org/enhanced-bedroom-ventilation-linked-to-improved-sleep-quality/).

However, the effect is conditional. A Shanghai study cited by the Sleep Foundation found that while opening windows improved indoor air quality, actual sleep quality did not improve in summer, because open windows also let in heat and outdoor noise — offsetting the ventilation benefit (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed).

## Bottom line

Opening a window/door improves ventilation and lowers CO2, which is genuinely linked to better sleep and next-day cognitive performance — but real-world benefits depend on outdoor temperature, noise, and pollution levels. The claim is broadly true, not false, but oversimplified without those caveats.
